stimulus.t: After the Bank of Aldonia cut its policy interest rate by a full percentage point,
the interest rates that Aldonian banks charged on new long-term mortgages rose.

stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Mortgage rates in several neighboring countries also rose during the same period.
Most outstanding Aldonian mortgages carry fixed rather than variable interest rates.
During the same period, yields on Aldonia’s long-term government bonds, to which mortgage rates are closely tied, rose sharply as investors came to expect higher inflation.
The rate cut was intended to stimulate borrowing by households and businesses.
Demand for new mortgages fell in the months following the rate cut.

tension: The central bank cut its policy rate

brief.facts: The policy rate fell, yet new long-term mortgage rates rose.
brief.rule: Resolve answers introduce a factor that allows both facts to coexist. They do not deny either fact.

analysis.correct: (C) Long-term mortgage rates track long-term bond yields, not just the short policy rate. If inflation expectations pushed long yields up, mortgage rates could rise despite the cut.

wrong.label: irrelevant-comparison
wrong.why: Shows it happened elsewhere but not WHY.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Concerns OUTSTANDING mortgages; the puzzle is about rates on NEW ones.

wrong.label: opposite
wrong.why: Restates the expectation that makes the result surprising, which deepens the puzzle.

wrong.label: opposite
wrong.why: Falling demand would, if anything, push rates down, which deepens the puzzle.

brief.holding: Good resolutions name a second mechanism that overrides the expected one.

stimulus.t: Judges who complete extensive training on cognitive biases rate themselves as far more aware of such biases than untrained judges do.

Yet in controlled experiments, trained judges’ sentencing decisions are just as influenced by irrelevant anchors, such as a randomly generated number shown before sentencing, as untrained judges’ decisions are.

stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the findings described above?
choices: Training programs on cognitive bias are expensive to administer.
Among trained judges, some were influenced by anchors less than others.
Awareness that a bias exists does not, by itself, give a person any means of correcting for it at the moment of decision.
Randomly generated numbers are seldom presented to judges in actual cases.
Untrained judges are less willing than trained judges to admit that they might be biased.

brief.facts: Training increases self-reported awareness of bias but does not reduce anchoring in experiments.
brief.issue: Why would more awareness not reduce the bias?
brief.rule: Resolve the gap between what one would expect (aware → less biased) and what happened.

analysis.correct: (C) If awareness supplies no in-the-moment correction mechanism, increased awareness and unchanged anchoring fit together.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Cost is irrelevant.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Variation within the trained group does not explain the group-level result.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Real-world frequency does not explain the experimental result.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Explains the self-ratings at most, not why behavior is unchanged.

brief.holding: When knowledge does not change behavior, the resolution usually separates knowing from doing.

stimulus.t: For decades, the number of taxi licenses in Varnia was capped.
When the cap was lifted, the number of taxis rose by 60 percent within two years,
yet average taxi fares did not decline.

stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?
choices: Some new taxi operators offered discounts to attract regular customers.
Many passengers complained about long waits for taxis before the cap was lifted.
Before the cap was lifted, taxi licenses were bought and sold for high prices.
Most new taxi drivers had previously worked in other transportation jobs.
Over the same two years, fuel prices and the cost of mandatory insurance for taxi operators roughly doubled.

brief.facts: More taxis (more competition) but no drop in fares.
brief.issue: What would keep fares up despite more competition?
brief.rule: Find a countervailing force that offsets the expected effect.

analysis.correct: (E) Sharply higher operating costs would push fares up, offsetting the competitive pressure to lower them.

wrong.label: opposite
wrong.why: Discounts push fares down, which deepens the puzzle.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Past waits do not explain post-reform fares.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Past license prices are sunk; they do not explain current fares.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Drivers’ backgrounds do not affect fares.

brief.holding: Look for the offsetting force: rising costs, rising demand, or a regulatory floor.

stimulus.t: The tribunal should not have awarded damages to the investor.
The investor knew the political risks when it entered the market.
Knowing about political risk is not the same as consenting to arbitrary expropriation.
The investor was entitled to compensation.

stem: Katalin and Andrei disagree over whether
choices: the investor knew the political risks when it entered the market
investors should avoid markets with significant political risk
the expropriation of the investor’s assets was arbitrary
tribunals should consider political risk at all
the investor should have been awarded damages

diagram.gap: Should the investor have been awarded damages?

brief.facts: Katalin: no damages, because the investor knew the risks. Andrei: knowing the risk is not consent, so compensation was owed.
brief.issue: On which claim do they hold OPPOSITE views?
brief.rule: Point at Issue: both speakers must express an opinion, and the opinions must conflict.

analysis.correct: (E) Katalin says no damages; Andrei says the investor was entitled to compensation. Direct conflict.

wrong.label: half-right
wrong.why: Katalin asserts it; Andrei does not dispute it and seems to accept it.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Neither addresses investor strategy.

wrong.label: half-right
wrong.why: Andrei implies arbitrariness; Katalin never addresses it.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Neither addresses this general question.

brief.holding: Run the agree/disagree test on each answer: Katalin? Andrei? Only a ‘yes vs. no’ pair qualifies.

stimulus.t: Central banks should not hold equities in their reserves.
Equity prices are volatile, and a central bank whose reserves suddenly lose value may be unable to defend its currency.
Central banks with modest equity allocations have earned higher long-run returns on their reserves than those holding only government bonds, and higher returns build larger buffers over time.
A reserve portfolio’s value over a decade matters more than its volatility over a quarter.

stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Mira and Tomás disagree over whether
choices: a central bank whose reserves suddenly lose value may be unable to defend its currency
equity prices are volatile
central banks holding equities have earned higher long-run returns
central banks should hold government bonds in their reserves
the short-term volatility of equities is a decisive reason for central banks to exclude them from reserves

brief.facts: Mira: exclude equities because volatility could cripple currency defense. Tomás: long-run returns build buffers; decade-long value outweighs quarterly volatility.
brief.issue: What do they actually clash on?
brief.rule: Speakers often share facts and disagree about their WEIGHT. Look for the evaluative claim each takes a side on.

analysis.correct: (E) Mira treats volatility as decisive; Tomás says it matters less than long-run value. Their positions conflict on its weight.

wrong.label: half-right
wrong.why: Tomás never addresses currency defense directly.

wrong.label: half-right
wrong.why: Tomás does not deny volatility; he discounts it.

wrong.label: half-right
wrong.why: Mira never addresses returns.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Both seem to accept holding bonds.

brief.holding: Sophisticated disputes are about weighting, not facts. Find the claim about what matters MORE.

stimulus.t: Judges should interpret statutes in light of their purpose.
Otherwise, the literal words can produce results the legislature never intended.
When judges consult a statute’s purpose, they too often substitute their own policy preferences for the text that was actually enacted.
The text is the only reliable evidence of what the legislature decided, so judges should confine themselves to it.

stem: The point at issue between Zsófia and Pavel is whether
choices: judges should interpret statutes in light of their purpose
legislatures intend the results of the statutes they enact
the text of a statute is evidence of what the legislature decided
judges have policy preferences
literal readings of statutes can produce results the legislature did not intend

brief.facts: Zsófia favors purposive interpretation. Pavel says judges should confine themselves to the text.
brief.rule: Both must take opposing positions on the answer’s claim.

analysis.correct: (A) Zsófia says yes; Pavel says judges should confine themselves to the text, which means no.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Neither addresses this directly.

wrong.label: half-right
wrong.why: Pavel affirms it; Zsófia does not deny it.

wrong.label: half-right
wrong.why: Zsófia never addresses judges’ preferences.

wrong.label: half-right
wrong.why: Pavel never denies this.

brief.holding: Conclusions are the most reliable place to find the point at issue.

stimulus.t: The new disclosure rule will burden small issuers, since compliance requires expensive audits.
But investors deserve the information, so the rule is worth its cost.
The rule’s audit requirement is so costly that many small firms will simply stop issuing public securities, leaving investors with fewer choices.
The rule should be withdrawn.

stem: Hannah and Viktor are committed to agreeing with which one of the following?
choices: Complying with the rule will be costly for small issuers.
Many small firms will stop issuing public securities.
The benefits of the rule outweigh its costs.
The rule should be withdrawn.
Audits are the most effective means of ensuring accurate disclosure.

diagram.gap: Common ground: compliance is costly for small issuers.

brief.facts: Hannah grants the cost but defends the rule. Viktor stresses the cost and opposes the rule.
brief.rule: Point of Agreement: both speakers must express (or clearly commit to) the same view.

analysis.correct: (A) Hannah: ‘will burden small issuers … expensive audits.’ Viktor: ‘so costly.’ Both commit to costliness.

wrong.label: half-right
wrong.why: Viktor only.

wrong.label: half-right
wrong.why: Hannah only; Viktor disagrees.

wrong.label: half-right
wrong.why: Viktor only; Hannah disagrees.

wrong.label: out-of-scope
wrong.why: Neither says this.

brief.holding: Concessions are fertile ground for agreement: what one concedes, the other may assert.

stimulus.t: The court was wrong to approve the merger on the grounds that new competitors would quickly enter the market.
Entry requires costly licenses, and the merged firm will control 45 percent of the market, a share at which firms generally raise prices.
The court’s reasoning was unpersuasive; costly licenses will keep new firms out for years.
Yet approving the merger was correct, because the merged firm’s customers are large utilities with the bargaining power to resist price increases.

stem: The dialogue most strongly supports the claim that Eszter and Lorant agree that
choices: firms controlling 45 percent of a market generally raise prices
large utilities have the bargaining power to resist price increases
the court should have blocked the merger
new competitors are unlikely to enter the market quickly
the merged firm will raise its prices

diagram.gap: Both reject the court’s rapid-entry rationale.

brief.facts: Eszter: the approval was wrong; licenses block entry; a 45% share leads to price increases. Lorant: the court’s rationale fails because licenses block entry, but the approval was right because of buyer power.
brief.issue: What do both accept despite their different bottom lines?
brief.rule: Speakers who disagree about conclusions may share a premise. Find the overlapping claim.

analysis.correct: (D) Both cite costly licenses as keeping entrants out, so both reject quick entry.

wrong.label: half-right
wrong.why: Eszter only.

wrong.label: half-right
wrong.why: Lorant only.

wrong.label: half-right
wrong.why: Eszter’s view at most; Lorant says approval was correct.

wrong.label: half-right
wrong.why: Eszter implies it; Lorant denies it (buyer power resists increases).

brief.holding: Agreement often hides in the reasoning, not the conclusions.
